## Essential Problem

The essential problem is finding a website or institute that provides **integrated statistics on forecasting rainbow occurrences in different countries**. This information would be valuable for understanding the geographical and seasonal variations in rainbow frequency.

## Relevant Information

To address this question, we need to consider the following factors:

* **Rainbow formation:** Rainbows are formed when sunlight is refracted and reflected by water droplets in the atmosphere. This requires specific conditions, including:
    * **Sunlight:** The sun needs to be at a low angle in the sky, typically within 42 degrees of the horizon.
    * **Water droplets:** Rain or mist is necessary to provide the water droplets that act as prisms.
    * **Clear sky:** A clear sky opposite the sun is needed for the rainbow to be visible.
* **Geographic factors:** The frequency of rainbows varies depending on geographical factors such as:
    * **Latitude:** Higher latitudes generally experience more frequent rainbows due to the lower angle of the sun.
    * **Climate:** Regions with frequent rainfall and mist are more likely to have rainbows.
    * **Topography:** Mountainous regions can create more opportunities for rainbows due to the presence of clouds and water droplets.
* **Seasonal variations:** The frequency of rainbows also varies seasonally, with more rainbows typically occurring in spring and summer when there is more rainfall and sunlight.

## Potential Resources

Based on the above information, here are some potential resources that might provide integrated statistics on rainbow occurrences:

* **National meteorological agencies:** Many national meteorological agencies collect and analyze data on weather phenomena, including rainbows. They may have statistics on rainbow frequency for different regions within their country.
* **International organizations:** Organizations like the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) might have compiled global data on rainbow occurrences.
* **Scientific research papers:** Academic research on rainbows might provide insights into the geographical and seasonal variations in their occurrence.
* **Citizen science projects:** Projects that involve citizen participation in collecting data on rainbows, such as the Rainbow Chase project, could provide valuable information.

## Draft Answer

Unfortunately, I haven't been able to find a single website or institute that provides integrated statistics on rainbow occurrences across different countries. However, the following resources might be helpful:

* **National meteorological agencies:** Check the websites of national meteorological agencies in the countries you are interested in. They may have data on rainbow frequency or be able to provide guidance on where to find such information.
* **International organizations:** Contact the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) to inquire about their data holdings on rainbows.
* **Scientific research papers:** Search academic databases for research papers on rainbow formation and occurrence. These papers might provide insights into the geographical and seasonal variations in rainbow frequency.
* **Citizen science projects:** Participate in citizen science projects like the Rainbow Chase project to contribute to the collection of data on rainbow occurrences.

I hope this information is helpful. Please let me know if you have any further questions.
gold_answer:
$\begingroup$

A rainbow is not a physical object that has a position. It is an optical
phenomena that depends on your location relative to the sun and rain. If you
are standing where your eyes can intercept the colored light, you are standing
with your back to the sun and the sunlight is reflecting on raindrops in front
of you. Someone else standing in a different location would not necessarily
see a rainbow if they looked up at the same part of the sky.

From [ University of Illinois
](http://ww2010.atmos.uiuc.edu/\(Gh\)/guides/mtr/opt/wtr/rnbw/frm.rxml) :

> According to Descartes' calculations using laws of optics, the three stage
> refraction-reflection-refraction pattern that light undergoes when passing
> through a raindrop produces a concentration of outgoing rays along a line
> that is 42 degrees above the head of an observer's shadow. This
> concentration of light rays is the rainbow that we see.

Also [ this National Geographic article
](https://www.nationalgeographic.org/encyclopedia/rainbow/print/#:%7E:text=In%20fact%2C%20no%20one%20sees,his%20or%20her%20own%20horizon.)
has a nice description:

> Viewers on the ground can only see the light reflected by raindrops above
> the horizon. Because each person's horizon is a little different, no one
> actually sees a full rainbow from the ground. In fact, no one sees the same
> rainbow—each person has a different antisolar point, each person has a
> different horizon. Someone who appears below or near the "end" of a rainbow
> to one viewer will see another rainbow, extending from his or her own
> horizon.

What this means is that a rainbow is not really a meteorological occurrence
that can be measured or catalogued, because you would get a different answer
depending on your reference point. Lightning, in contrast, is a physical
phenomena that has a precise location which can be determined and verified
from multiple points of reference.

Rainbows are photographed and archived by enthusiasts, but it's really about
artistic appreciation. While I have not looked into rainbow forecast services,
a quick search shows some interesting resources, such as [ How to Predict
Rainbows and Plan Photographs ](https://stephenbayphotography.com/blog/how-to-
predict-rainbows-and-plan-photographs/) which has a link to a [ photography
app that can plan for rainbows ](https://www.planitphoto.com/#feature) and
here is a [ rainbow app you can install
](http://www.erikscarlson.com/project/chance-of-
rainbow#:%7E:text=Creating%20an%20algorithm%20to%20predict,\(if%20that%20is%20possible\).)
on your phone.

[ How Rainbows Happen ](http://www.rebeccapaton.net/rainbows/formatn.htm) also
has a nice description (shown below) and some other useful resources. [
![enter image description here](https://i.sstatic.net/GEDyn.gif)
](https://i.sstatic.net/GEDyn.gif)
